evidence.claim: The Mills Scenic Byway links river crossings and mill towns with rolling farmland, woods and stone walls.
evidence.quote: views of rolling open hills bordered by forest and stone walls cut through by brooks and low-lying wetland marshes

evidence.claim: It follows local streets and NH 4 in Rollinsford, then NH 108 through Madbury, Durham and Newmarket, with a break in the byway through Dover.
evidence.quote: The byway stops here and picks up in Madbury on Route 108 but it easy to continue through Dover along Route 108 to join the next leg of the route.

evidence.claim: Its 2016 corridor management plan identifies scenic, natural, historic, cultural, archaeological and recreational qualities, with nineteenth-century textile mills as the common thread.
evidence.quote: The history of the 19th century textile mills is the common element found along the byway.

evidence.claim: The corridor plan grew from work begun in 2009 and resumed in 2011 and 2014.
evidence.quote: Management Plan initially began in early 2009. It protection efforts; however, they do not have any was picked back up in 2011 and again in 2014.

evidence.claim: The four towns worked with the Strafford Regional Planning Commission to form a byway committee and hold public meetings.
evidence.quote: SRPC worked with all four towns to form a Byway interpret, and promote the intrinsic qualities of designated Committee and held a series of public meetings.

evidence.claim: Their purpose was to balance promotion with protection of the corridor’s resources.
evidence.quote: The purpose of creating such a plan is to identify ways that the four communities can collaborate to strike a balance between promotion and protection of the byway’s resources.

evidence.claim: The resulting plan was adopted in October 2016.
evidence.quote: 2016 Corridor Management Plan Adopted 10/17/2016

evidence.claim: Start at the South Berwick boundary on Front Street in Rollinsford, continuing by Main Street and Roberts Road to NH 4.
evidence.quote: Starting at the northern end, the route starts at the border of South Berwick Maine, and Front Street in Rollinsford, New Hampshire. Continuing south from Front Street, the route turns right onto Main Street, and continues onto Roberts Road where the route intersects with NH Route 4, Portland Ave.

evidence.claim: NH 108 connects the gap through Dover to the next byway segment in Madbury.
evidence.quote: The byway stops here and picks up in Madbury on Route 108 but it easy to continue through Dover along Route 108 to join the next leg of the route.

evidence.claim: Continue through Durham across the Oyster River, then through Newmarket beside the Lamprey, ending at the Newfields town line.
evidence.quote: The byway follows Route 108 through Durham and into Newmarket where the route ends at the town line of Newmarket and Newfields.

evidence.claim: scenic, natural, historic, cultural, archaeological and recreational qualities
evidence.quote: Scenic, Natural, Historic, Cultural, Archeological, and Recreational. The Mills Scenic Byway possesses noteworthy qualities of all six resources.

evidence.claim: Continue through Durham across the Oyster River
evidence.quote: As the byway continues, it passes over the beautiful Oyster River

evidence.claim: On Front Street, the Salmon Falls mill complex occupies a site where an earlier woolen factory burned in 1834.
evidence.quote: It burned in 1834, but was soon replaced by a cotton mill.

evidence.claim: Cotton manufacturing followed, and the Number 2 Mill, built in 1848, used a turbine instead of a waterwheel to power its machinery.
evidence.quote: The Number 2 Mill, built in 1848, was an early location where a turbine was used instead of a waterwheel to provide power to the mill machinery.

evidence.claim: The mill buildings are predominantly brick, with additions designed to match the existing structures.
evidence.quote: with most buildings built of brick in an industrial Italianate style.

evidence.claim: Beyond the mills, a section of NH 4 parallels the Newichawannock trail, a Native American roadway predating 1600 that Revolutionary War soldiers used between Maine, New Hampshire and Boston.
evidence.quote: a pre- 1600 Native American roadway used by Revolutionary War soldiers traveling from Maine and New Hampshire to Boston.

evidence.claim: with additions designed to match the existing structures.
evidence.quote: additions made to the buildings were done with attention to matching design elements from the existing structures.

evidence.claim: a section of NH 4 parallels the Newichawannock trail
evidence.quote: There is also a section of Route 4 in Rollinsford that runs parallel to the Newichawannock trail;

evidence.claim: At Durham’s Oyster River crossing, the Jenkins mill occupied the dam site in the mid-1800s.
evidence.quote: the Oyster River Ambursen Dam was the site of the Old Jenkins Mill in the mid-1800s.

evidence.claim: Decay and the weight of snow eventually brought it down, reportedly in about 1955.
evidence.quote: This mill stood until it eventually collapsed from decay and the weight of snow, reportedly in about 1955.

evidence.claim: The historic district extends along NH 108 and Main Street, with the Oyster River running through it.
evidence.quote: The Durham Historic District encompasses a portion of the original historic settlement area of Durham, New Hampshire.

evidence.claim: This settlement developed into a shipbuilding center in the eighteenth century.
evidence.quote: It was developed in the 18th century as a significant shipbuilding center.

evidence.claim: South of the river, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century houses line Newmarket Street; the Durham Community Church, built in 1848–49, anchors the district’s Main Street section.
evidence.quote: Along Newmarket Street stand a row of 18th and 19th-century houses just south of the Oyster River.

evidence.claim: The historic district extends along NH 108 and Main Street, with the Oyster River running through it.
evidence.quote: It extends along Newmarket Road (New Hampshire Route 108) from its northern junction with Laurel Lane to a three-way junction with Main Street and Dover Road (the latter being the continuation of NH 108).  From there it extends along Main Street to Madbury Road.

evidence.claim: the Durham Community Church, built in 1848–49, anchors the district’s Main Street section.
evidence.quote: the Durham Community Church, built in 1848–49, which is the focal point of the Main Street section of the district.

evidence.claim: Newmarket’s mills made an unusual choice of building material: granite rather than the brick used in the Waltham factories they followed.
evidence.quote: Despite being modeled after the factories in the Waltham system, the most significant difference was the use of granite instead of brick

evidence.claim: By 1832, three mills were operating with 13,824 spindles.
evidence.quote: By 1832 three mills were completed and in full operation, containing a total of 13,824 spindles

evidence.claim: Stone also appears in the town’s houses, churches and schools.
evidence.quote: The use of stone was not limited to the mills themselves: the historic district also has examples of stone houses, churches, and schools.

evidence.claim: Surviving mills line the Lamprey River along the eastern side of the historic district.
evidence.quote: Its principal eastern boundary is the Lamprey River, along which the surviving mill buildings are arrayed.

evidence.claim: Madbury brings undulating hills and farm country; houses from the late 1700s and early 1800s once belonged to some of the town’s largest dairy farms.
evidence.quote: As a byway user crosses into Madbury the landscape opens up into undulating hills and local farmland. Here one will find a number of houses that were built in the late 1700s to the early 1800s and were homes to some of the largest dairy farms in the town.

evidence.claim: White church steeples, mill buildings and riverfront parks punctuate the downtown districts.
evidence.quote: downtown historic districts peppered with white church steeples, old mill buildings, river frontage, and park areas

evidence.claim: The Salmon Falls Manufacturing Company stopped production in 1927. The mills now contain artists’ and artisans’ studios, including spaces for painting and furniture making.
evidence.quote: The Salmon Falls Manufacturing Company ended production in 1927

evidence.claim: The mills now contain artists’ and artisans’ studios, including spaces for painting and furniture making.
evidence.quote: Today, the mills have been reborn as low-cost studio space for more than 100 artists and artisans who use the converted studios for everything from painting, sculpting and crafting handmade furniture

evidence.claim: The 2016 Mills Scenic Byway Corridor Management Plan recorded the mill foundation as remaining at the dam site.
evidence.quote: The foundation remains today.

evidence.claim: Commercial buildings stand across Main Street from the mills, with residential buildings on the side streets.
evidence.quote: Commercial buildings are mainly located across Main Street from the mills, with residential housing on side streets.

evidence.claim: To keep the mills running through drought, the company built upstream dams and released stored water into the Lamprey as needed.
evidence.quote: The company built dams far upriver to create Pawtuckaway Pond in Nottingham and Mendums Pond in Barrington—during drought, the company could release a regulated flow of water from the dams into the Lamprey to run the works.

evidence.claim: The historic district extends along NH 108 and Main Street, with the Oyster River running through it.
evidence.quote: for the Oyster River which bisects it

evidence.claim: On Front Street, the Salmon Falls mill complex
evidence.quote: The Salmon Falls Mill Historic District encompasses a historic mill complex on Front Street in Rollinsford, New Hampshire.

evidence.claim: an earlier woolen factory burned in 1834.
evidence.quote: In 1822 the water privilege was purchased by a Portsmouth merchant, who established a successful woolen mill.  It burned in 1834

evidence.quote: Traveling north on Route 108 in Newmarket the byway winds through the downtown and passes both Arbor and Schanda Parks. Together they offer remarkable views of the tidal portion of the Lamprey River

flags: The 2016 plan calls this a byway but its signage section still describes state acceptance as prospective. The cache does not resolve final state designation, so no designation date or confirmed present state status is asserted.

Material’s strip miles put Newmarket before Durham; the plan’s explicit north-to-south route and cached town geography establish Rollinsford, Dover connection, Madbury, Durham, Newmarket. Used that driving order.

The 2016 plan is the only cache source for the Oyster River dam/foundation and Lamprey weir viewing claims. Omitted present visibility/access promises and retained the Jenkins mill history with the source’s reportedly in about qualification.
Newmarket sources disagree on mill closure: 1920 in the district article versus 1929 in the town article. Closure date omitted.

The plan uses Swamscott while other cached material uses other regional names. The weir’s tribal attribution is omitted pending a community or archaeological source; the Newichawannock trail name follows the plan.
